name: decapitation
sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Decapitation of enemies carried deep meaning for the Celts. Greek and Roman writers recorded the practice in Gaul. The Gauls cut the heads from their slain enemies and hung them from the necks of their horses. They nailed the finest spoils to their house walls and preserved the heads of distinguished enemies in cedar oil. Keepers refused ransom for these heads even when offered gold. The head may have been seen as the seat of the soul, warding off evil and giving the keeper the wisdom of the dead man. Severed heads also guarded sacred places. At Roquepertuse, a stone portico set human skulls in carved niches. The sanctuary at Entremont raised a pillar carved with twelve severed heads. The tales of the Ulster Cycle carry the same motif, and Cú Chulainn took enemy heads as war trophies.
objective: Records the severed head as a sacred Celtic symbol of power and decapitation as a cult practice.
key_results: Greek and Roman authors described Gaulish head-hunting and the display of severed heads.
The portico at Roquepertuse set human skulls in carved stone niches.
Keepers of heads refused gold even when offered as ransom of equal weight.
The Ulster Cycle features heroes who take enemy heads as trophies.
